blocks.x: What would you like to turn off your name if you like, Arch?
Well, my name is Arthur Frank Hazel. I was born in Harvey, Louisiana. That's just across from Louisiana Avenue in New Orleans.
What was the date?

August the 15th, 1903. My father was a bass drummer in one of the early jazz bands of New Orleans. It was called Fish's Ragtime Military Jazz Band. And my first teacher was Rag Baby Stevens. And my first job was in the carnival parade. In those days the only parade that had any jazz in it at all was the Rex parade, which was a union. The only union parade of all the parades.
How many of those bands would really swing there in the Rex parade?

Well, the Fish's Band was the only band in the whole parade that swang. Incidentally, it was all white bands. The Fish's Band was the only band in the parade that swang. And in the band was two of the Brunus boys, Henry and Richard. And a clarinet player who played E-flat clarinet instead of the traditional B-flat. His name was Ashil Bakay. And Happy Shilling was in that band. Johnny Fisher. Cack Riley was a trombone player. Henry Brunus was alto horn. And Richie played cornet. And a fellow by the name of Marlow on the other cornet. My dad on bass drum, Rag Baby Stevens, and myself on snare drum. What was your dad's full name? Charles. Charles Henry. Can you tell us about how old he was when he died?
Do you know his birth date too, roughly?
He was 58 when he died. And he died in 1939. Now that, the boy thought not.
That'll dig again. Yeah. And he played, just the, he didn't play the double drums at all.

As you know in those days, even for the dance jobs they used double drums instead of traps. And he had a single dash on his drums. And he played, just the, he didn't play the double drums at all. As you know in those days, even for the dance jobs they used double drums instead of traps. Yeah, with the, with the wire hat band and a hard rubber ball for the beater. And here's a little story that happened in this first parade that I ever played. The parades in those days started at Calliope in St. Charles because all the dens were back Calliope street then. And you'd come out and farm at Calliope in St. Charles and you'd come up to Washington Avenue on the right hand side. And then turn around and come back to the left side to Canal street. And then you went to the opera house. You didn't go like they, like they do now. Well anyway, we got around Malpamine in St. Charles and I was on the outside. And they had a little thing called a torpedo stick. It was a, a stick. And it had a little iron thing on the bottom of it. And you'd put a cap in there, a torpedo. Well, that little jig kid hit me on the foot with this, well he wasn't so, he wasn't so sweet. He was much, but I mean a kid around 14, 15 years old. And he hit me on the foot with this torpedo thing. That was a favorite sport around Mardi Gras that on Canal street along the parade routes, you know. And I didn't see him at all, but Rag Baby spied him. So when we come around, we're coming down when we got near Malpamine, Rag Baby made me get in the middle. And he got on the outside and he took the bass drum and handed my dad his drum. And he had that hard rubber ball and he's looking for this kid all the time. And he fired, he spied him when we got right near there. And he wrapped him across the head with that rubber ball. Well that was, that was my first.
It didn't burn your foot I guess? Did it burn?

No, no it hurt. It hurt, but it didn't burn. That way, you see, they were made, it was a little bag, like a paper bag like that. And it had with a little round pellets like that. And when they went, when you'd hit him, it hit him on the ground that would discharge it and they would spread. These little pellets would spread all around. And if they hit you in the leg, something like that, they would burn.

Well I was going to ask about the position of the bass drummer. Was he always on the left? Always on the left, as a rule. As you marched on the left, as a rule. Yeah. The bass drummer is over on your left and you were the snare drum on the right.

Unless you like, like we here, you had two and then you put the other one in the middle. And then, in those days the trombones, and if you had two trombones, well you'd have the two trombones and the bass horn. Incidentally, in this vicious band, there's a musician who became later a legitimate musician in the Sanger Theater. He became an old boss, by the name of Alessandra. He was also a peck horn player in that band and his father was a bass player. He had one of these Italian helican basses, not the Sousa for him, but the old helican bass. He was in the band also.
Did he have any saxes in the band in those days?

No, no. In those days there was only one saxophone player in New Orleans. He came here with a Mexican national band, a Mexican government band. His name was Remus. And he came here and although he was an old man at that time, he played with Tony Perranti. But when he originally came here, he was the only saxophone player in New Orleans. And then later on there was a fellow by the name of Dan Sanderson who played saxophone. But in those days, that's far back, they always used clarinets, no saxophones. But the, of the younger generation, but the first one I know of that played saxophone was little George, young George Shilling, Happy Shilling's son. And he started, oh, very, ten, eight, around eleven to twelve years old playing saxophone in his daddy's band. But, uh...

Did you ever hear any more else, anything else about that old Mexican band, your father talked about it? You know, um, um, Jack Lane says his father bought some of the old instruments and some drums from that band for him and some old flags. That's how he got started.

Well, that's, that's, that's possible, that's possible, but, uh, I don't think my dad ever, ever knew anything about that band. The only reason I happened to know about it was, uh, was from old man Ramis himself. Yeah. And that had been several years after he, he'd, uh, settled here with that band. Uh, and, and, and in that band, uh, they had another man who stayed here. Uh, uh, he was, he was, uh, the solo cornetist in this band. His name was Lopez. Oh. He was, uh, sort of on, on, uh, on the art of, uh, this, uh, fellow in New York who's so well-known, makes records and everything.
Like Del Stegas?

Del Stegas, that, that, that thing. And he stayed here also, not very long. He stayed here for a couple of years and played in a couple of, I think he played with Happy Schilling. Yeah. And, uh, but he didn't stay around very long. But old man, Ramis, I think, stayed here until he died. And he worked with, with Tony Peretti at the, the Vita there.
What's his name anyway? Full name, do you remember? Ramis?

Uh huh. I wouldn't know, Dick, I wouldn't know he's, he's, he's full. That's the only thing I can remember. Tony could tell, could tell you all about it. Oh yeah. Because he worked with Tony for, for a number of years at that, the Vita.
Oh, by the way, what about Rag Baby Steelers? Who did he play with mostly?

Well, he played, he played with, with Fishers Band and he played, yeah, imagine he played with Lane and all the early bands. The Harmony Band and, and, and a fella by the name of Cock Eye Hughes. A cornet player had a band. And, and, and, and the Christians had a band. And, and, and, uh. Bronze was a, a favorite band. And these are, like, like, I explained to you Bill, how they call them ragtime military jazz bands. They, they played a little bit of, of everything. If it was a picnic, they'd play jazz. And they played for dances all around? Oh yes, yes, and just dances and picnics. They had a lot of lodges around here like the Pithians, Knights, Knights of Columbus, the Moose. And each, each, each, and the BKVs, each lot had its own hall, you know, where it assembled. And they always had a, a dance, a very good dance floor, where they, where they gave dances. And, uh.
When you played the dances, they used the snare drum and the bass drum too?

Well, when I first started, yes. Because, uh, another little story about Rag Baby. Uh, incidentally, he has a son who works in the quarter. Yeah. Yeah. Nah. Well, Rag Baby was, uh, he always had, uh, lady troubles. And, uh, he, he was, uh, he, he left his family. I think he had six, seven kids, something like that. And he left to pull out on the family. And the, the police were always hounding him, you know, for alimony. And, uh, my dad would have to carry me along because they, they had places like the Southern Park out, out, out near, uh, by St. John there. And he's picking up over the river at the, the Crescent Park. And, uh, there was no telling when the detectives were gonna show up and Rag Baby would have to jump over the fence and take off, you see. And then I'd have to, I'd have to finish the night for him. And, uh, uh, he, uh, then he left here and he went to Chicago. He was around Chicago for a good while. He opened up a music shop up there. And he was the kind of guy that if he came out to his, out to see him and he had a silk Pangee suit on or something like, which was style in those days, Shantong, you know. Yeah. You had something wrong with your automobile, he'd just jump underneath there with that silk suit on and then see what's the matter with it. And he finally got killed in an automobile accident in Chicago. Yeah. And he was, a very fine drummer, both parade and, and jazz. He was, uh, uh, well, among the musicians, he, he was, uh, better thought of as, as a jazz drummer than, than Stein, who was the guy in the palace who has all the reputation. But the, the, the thing with Stein was that he had, uh, he had nine pipes built in a, in a U shape and he had, oh, everything in the world. Yeah. And the chimes and the, the boats and whistles and the bells and everything. He had everything in the world on that thing. But the, uh, uh, Rag Baby was more of a drummer, not a, not a showman. Like the, the solos today, things like that. Well, he was more of a, of a band. He worked for the band rather than for himself.
Well, before I forget, you mentioned that, uh, word double drums. I've heard Papa Lane talk about that. Just what do you mean?

Well, instead of having one man play both drums, you know, with the foot pedal and that, well, you had, you had two men. One played the bass drum and one played the snare drum. Not only in parades, now this was for any, any, any dances at all. Because there was no such thing as the foot pedal there.
Yeah. So when they used double drums, they used two men.
They used two men. Yeah. That's, what I meant by.
I didn't know something. Could've meant that one guy played two drums, snare and the bass.
No, no. The same number. No. No. And, uh, when, uh, when, uh, when the, when the, when the foot pedals first came out and, uh, and, uh, and, uh, then you could use the traps. They called them traps.
Yeah.

You didn't call them accessories. They called them traps. And you could, uh, you could use the cymbal on top and, and, and, and the, and the foot pedal. And they always had a little, a little, a little attachment on, on the, on the pedal there. And you'd put a cymbal down on the side of the bass drum and it would hit the, hit the bass drum and the cymbal simultaneously like that. You know, to give that, that little whatchacom. And, uh, there's no, no such thing as, uh, is, uh, hi-hats or anything like that. Cause the first, the first, uh, the things that resembled hi-hats at all were, were, uh, Ray Badu, uh, designed the first one that I've ever seen in my life. There was two cymbals with a, with a pedal, but down, not, not up like they are now, but down, down, down, down like that. And they would hit together like that.
Just about a foot off the floor?

Just about a foot off the floor, yeah. And Ray designed the first one that I've ever seen. And I think it was Ludwig, old man Ludwig, you know, the WFL. I think he was the one who put the first one out. And then later came the, the, the hi-hat. But then they, they, they'd call you, if you played, uh, the, the both drums at one time, they'd call you a trap drum in those days, you see.
What all did you use in the way of wood blocks or cowbells and so on?
Well, we used to use all of those things and, uh, tom-toms, the, the old, the old style, not the, not the tunable.
The Chinese.

Yeah, the old Chinese. And, uh, and the, the, the, the old Chinese crash was always, for jazz, was always a thing. And then later on, they came out with the Sildjans. And, uh, I never did stop using the crash. And, uh, the, then later on, they put the rivets in the, in the, the old Chinese crash, like the one I, I had when I first recorded with Sharky. For about the first five years. And then, that famous store, I got sick and was laid up for a while and somebody stole it. I never been able to get one with it. Just that right tone. Yeah. It was a, it was a, it was a 22 inch one. Yet, it, but it didn't make too much noise. Wasn't too loud. And it, it didn't ring too, too much. You know, it wouldn't ring over into the next measure. Yeah. Yeah. Oh if you, if you hit it, would just last that, that shh would just last just long enough. So they wouldn't, like these new ones that, these Sildjans things hit, they just keep rolling and rolling. You know. There's no, no distinction in the beats.
So I'm trying to ask about the bass drum. How big a bass drum did they use in the old days?

big drums or smaller drums? Well for the dance jobs they used the bigger drums. They ran anywhere from 12 inches to 16. I had a 16 by 30. About 30 inches and really a big drum. And 16 inches wide. But the standard was the 1428. But for parades, some of the guys used to use these little narrow things about 8 inches, about 28. You know most of the colored fellas used those.
They still used about 28 on the parades.
Yeah.
Mark, do you remember the first foot pedal for the bass drum that you ever saw? Yeah. About when?

I can't remember when, the date, but I can describe it to you. It had a long metal rod. And on the end of the rod was the beater. And then there was a, in the end of the beater, there was a little screw thing that was sort of a, triangle in shape. And you fit a leather strap through that. And you fit a leather strap through that. And you fit a stuff the foot part of it was wood, well that hooked into like a, oh like these, anything that you, like the mailman's straps, you know, a deal like that, and then it hooked into the pedal, and the pedal was, had a metal housing, you might call it, and then to get the leverage, the spring was on the top of the bass drum, and it fit into a hole in this long rod, in one end of the spring, and the other end, it had like a fork, that would fit on the shell, the rim of the bass drum, like that, to keep it steady, you see, and you could, they had a, a tension knot on there, where you could loosen it, or tighten it to your individual taste, and that's, that's, that, I think, I'm not positive, but I think that was the first foot pedal ever made, I mean that's, that's, that's the way, that's the first one I ever saw, Which head did it hit? That's the way it was, huh? Which head did it hit? Which head of the drum did it hit? The inside, the inside, the inside, did it hit from above? It hit in the, exactly in the middle, but the, the leverage was from above, yeah, the spring, you see, the spring was, was, and when, when, if you hit it, well then, when you let it go, it would, but the spring, didn't, well it was not built into the pedal, it was on the top of the bass drum, and, and, and, fit into a hole, and, in this, this long, uh, rod, and that the ball, was on the end of that rod, and then the bottom of the ball, like I tell you, had this little thing where you fit the strap into, and the strap in turn fit into the, into the wooden pedal, the wooden pedal, and that, the wooden pedal, was held by, a, steel frame, or iron frame, whatever it was, that's the earliest pedal that I can recall, there may be a couple of them around here, yeah, some of the real old timers, should, should, should have one of them, Did you have, no, I don't think he, they might pick one up, you know, I'll tell you, there's only, there's only, there's only about one fellow that I know of, around here, who might have one, Bill, there's a fellow by the name of Emil Gonzalez,
Is he still alive?

I don't know, but he would, because he, he used to fix all of our heads, tuck our heads, and, and fix all of our drums for, for us, you know, he, he, he was the man. How was the action, did you ever play around, did it sing fast, or, oh, well, you, like I tell you, they had a, they had a, what's called them that you could regulate it, the way you, But it was, very, it was very shaky, Bill, you see?
Not like the modern.

No, it wasn't, it, it, it wasn't compact, and naturally, so it was shaky, and it was the only way that they could, in those days, the only way they could build, But you couldn't, you couldn't, when you, when you'd hit down like that, it would, it, this, the bottom part of it, they would shake like that, and it wasn't reliable, like the, later pedals became.
Where's Emil Gonzalez's family? Are they around, you know?

They did live on Gainia Street somewhere, out around, none say, around Constance Street, between Constance and Chapitulis. At Gainia? Yeah, in Gainia, G-A-I-N-I-E, Gainia, that's, that's just a couple of blocks up from, it's a little short street, it only runs to, it stops at Magazine Street, it runs from the river to Magazine Street. It's about the, about the 1200, about the 11 or 1200 block, coming up from Canal Street, and he may have one, because he had everything, he was a guy like Tom Brown, that collected everything, you know, and he had everything that you could ever imagine, that pertained to drums, and he, incidentally, was a very good mechanic, he could do more with it, and he, of course, in those days, everything was wood, too, no metal drums.
Speaking of Tom Brown, when was the first time you heard him or his band?

Tom, well, no, when, when, when I started, Tom was away. I didn't meet Tom till, till he came back to New Orleans, and the first time I played with Tom was with Brownlee's band, out at the old Spanish fort, and, and then, while I was, I think it was a couple of years after or before that, I was working with Abby Burns out at the halfway house, when his brother Theodore came down here, with a bunch of guys from Chicago, Murphy Steinberg, and, uh, was it Polo, Polo, Clarinet player, Danny Polo, Danny Polo, something like that. They were, they were, they had a band that they patterned off of the, off of the rhythm games. So, now, the, the, after, to follow up on that, that first job thing, after that, we moved from Harvard, we moved down to Gretton, and that's where I met Emmett Hardy, I went to school with, with Emmett, you see, and we formed a little band around Gretton, and he used to play across the river. We didn't get older than New Orleans, only on one job.
How old is Hardy? Was he older than you, or?
Uh, he was, no, he, he was, he was younger than me. Let's see, he died in, he died in 25, and he was 21 when he died.

Uh, but he covered a lot of ground in, in those years, and he used to make it, he made his own mop pieces. He, he worked in the, machine shop, and his, his, his brother, uh, today is head of this Bishop Edel machine company here, and he wanted him to be a machinist. Emmett didn't care about machinists, he, he wanted to play music. So he'd work all day in the fountain, and he made, he made his own mouth pieces. It was always experimenting, like Jack Teagarden, you know, always experimenting. I think he had a little engineer in him, frustrated engineer in him. And, uh, uh, uh, we had a little band over there, Sidney Arden, and, uh, Emmett, and Brownlee, and, uh, the kid that, that died at 16 years old was, would have been a marvelous trombone player by the name of Fort Myer. He had a brother who played cornet trumpet that you, you fellas, you might know of, Dick. He's from Jefferson, Paris. He played all these places along. Raymond talks about it. Yeah, Fort Myer. Fort Myer, they used to call him, but it's really Fort Myer. And, uh, he played beautiful from all. He had beautiful, uh, tones sort of like, like Santo, but better. Uh, you know, clearer, prettier. And he died when he was 16. And we were all just kids, and we played around, up and down, over the hill.
Tell more about Emmett, um, how he got, did he ever tell you how he got started on the cornet? Did he use cornet or trumpet?

Well, his daddy, his daddy was a bass player in the, in the shrine band. Here, you see, and that's where, and his mother played piano. And, uh, they used to sit around at home and play, and that's how he, he never did play, well, he played, he started with a guitar. And a banjo.
Yeah.

And then, and then that, they didn't like that so much. And even a little piano, according, and his mother played in, played real fine church piano, you know. And, uh, his sister played piano and sang, uh, spirituals. And he had an uncle who's quite well known as an author. His name is Kennedy, Emmett Kennedy. He's written a lot of books and things like that. And he was, he was a piano player, too. It's just natural in, in the family, you see. And, uh, then, once he hit the carnet, well, and he, and he never did play trumpet. He played carnet. They went to, he and, he and, uh, when he was with the Rhythm Kings, he and Paul Morez and Chink Martin went to this higher B.J. company. And, and, and they had a, uh, uh, he and Paul both had an instrument made called, uh, it was a, you could make it either a trumpet or a carnet. It had a, it had a, uh, the mouth pipe, you know. Yeah. And you could pull it out or shove it in. And you could make it either a trumpet or a carnet. And they had them custom, custom made, you know. It was something new and then nobody had seen anything like that. And, uh, but he, he, he never did like the, the, the trumpet sound. He always liked the, the cornet sound. And he always played the cornet. And, uh, and, uh.
Did you know he had any lessons around here? He studied from Manuel Mineta.

The, the, the old colored fellow over here. He studied from Manuel Mineta. And, uh, this thing on high society. You know, the, the, da, The baronet variation. Well, that's, that belongs to Manuel Mineta. Manuel Mineta, uh, created that, or whatever you want to call it. He was the first one to play it. And he taught it to Emmett. And, uh, and, uh, and he and Emmett are the only two ones that I ever heard play it that play it right. All the rest of them, and that, that includes Shark and, and all of them, all the rest of them.
How does this play?
Don't play it right. It doesn't go, it doesn't, it doesn't go like they play it. It,
It's not the clarinet solo, it's a trumpet.
It's a trumpet. You know, the, da, Oh, you mean on Panama? Now they play it, you know, Panama. Panama, yeah. Panama, yeah.
Panama, yeah.

They, play it three ways now. Yeah. Uh, well, uh, and he taught, Manuel taught it to, to Emmett, and Emmett's the only one, the only white man that I ever heard that plays right, exactly the way, uh, Manuel, because Manuel at that time was on the boat, you know, with, with fate. He was, all, he was playing melliform on the boat.
And, uh, you know, he told me, uh, Red Allen stole Emmett Hardy's book, that he wrote it out for him. Yeah, he, he did. He stole it and got that part.

He did, he, wrote it out for Emmett, and, and, and, and he, and he, and taught it to him to make sure that Emmett played it right, you know. And that, I, I know that to be a positive fact. And, uh, then later on, uh, uh, Hardy made up his own band over the river there. Mm-hmm. And, but the only time that we ever played, uh, uh, other than over the river, there, there was a place of a Sharky Stomp ground called the Taunty Social Club. And, uh, Sharky played back there for years. And, I don't know, they had a run in or something. Let me see.
That's right, now you're on a stop.
Yeah.
All right, okay, it's going again. You were talking about Emmett Hardy and this band, Sharky and the Taunty.

Well, uh, somehow or other, they, uh, they had a run in with a club. It was a club, a social club that, uh, that had this. It was the Taunty Aiden Social Club. And they had this hall. And, uh, they had a run in, so they fired Sharky. And they hired Hardy, you see. So we went over there. And, uh, they had a bandstand. And the bandstand was against the back wall. And they had a window, like that. Right in the back of the drums. And in those days, there weren't any sense. The first thing is spurs, Bill. You know, you had to take a rope and tie it around the chair. They keep the bass drum from walking away, you see. So, uh, Sharky's drummer was named Roy Montgomery. And he was Sharky's brother-in-law. Uh, nephew, rather. Their nephew. He was Sharky's sister's child. And, uh, the night that we started, uh, they were gonna create a free-for-all. Because nobody wanted to come in there and go Sharky, you know. So there was a little fella come up around 10.30. A little fella like I came up and he told us, he said, those guys are gonna lay for you. So they're gonna start a free-for-all, the first thing they're gonna do. And whenever a free-for-all would start, Bill, they'd turn the lights out and then the beer bottles would fly, you know. And, uh, they said, they're gonna lay for you. And in those days, the Chapitula streetcar ran from City Park to Audubon Park. You see, and, uh, this club was right off of Ursuline Street, the street that the Chapitula streetcar ran on. And, uh, they said, they're gonna lay for you guys. They said, no worry about, ain't nobody gonna hurt you. And we look at this little bit of guy, you know. And, uh, they did. But, uh, about quarter of the 12th, they started this free-for-all, you see. And they put the lights out and started throwing. Somebody hit me in the back of the head with the, with the beer bottles. And all those guys thought I was doing about the wind and went around the alley, you see. And I went there, I got caught up in that rope around the bass drum, you know. And, uh, and couldn't, couldn't find the wind. And that's how I come to get hit, hit in the head with the, with the beer bottles. And stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff

So then we finally got out and we were going to catch the streetcars because we were all from over the river. And those days there was always a feud going on between the guys from Algiers and the guys from New Orleans, the guys from Gretna and the guys from New Orleans. Or even from one neighborhood to the other. And always about 15 of them got around us. They wanted to know what we were doing, taking a shorty job and everything like that. And they were just about getting ready to... They'd always send a little guy to pick on you to make you mad, you know, enough to want to fight or get smart and then they'd rap you. And they were just about getting ready to rap us when this little fellow who had told us don't worry about anything comes out from a high box step across the street there. He comes out there and he got a smoke wagon on him about that long and he says, I dare one of y'all to touch him. He says, they got a better band than Sharky's got. You know, one of those things. And we finally got on the streetcar and got home. But we never did go back anymore. And then we had a job at a place over the river called the Midway. And they started playing... The last tune they started playing... They quit at quarter to twelve because you had to quit at quarter to twelve to catch the last streetcar to make the Jackson Ferry, you see. And they started playing the blues at eleven o'clock, you see. And they played the blues for forty-five minutes. They'd play them slow first and then medium tempo. And then what we called fast tempo in those days, not even medium now, you know. And they'd play the blues in those three different tempos. Well, that's when the free falls would start off. And it was an open air place. You see, no, no, it had a roof over it, but all the rest of it was open and had chicken wire in front of the bandstand so the beer bottles wouldn't hit the band. And things like that. And you'd have to fight your way through the fight to get out to get in the streetcar, you know. Oh, they had several of them over there like that. They had that Owls Hall on the river there. But, yeah, it was right just about a half a block down from Jackson Avenue. And a fella coming from New Orleans would come over and try to fool one of the girls there.
Across the river?

Well, this Owls Hall, it was just about a block down from the ferry landing. And they would do, if they caught you fooling, the fellas over there would go up the fellas from New Orleans fooling with any of the girls. Well, they'd do either one of two things. They'd either run them up the levee and down the ferry landing. If the ferry wasn't in, don't stop, just keep going, you know. Either that or the two fellas would get the guy, one by the arms and one by the legs and take him by a window like that and swing him like that. It was built on pilings right on the water, you see.
