And at that time Art Hickman was the rage. In California you see. So he wanted me to play music like Art Hickman. So. All we used to get up there was like I tell you. The college kids. And it was a dollar to get in and two cents tax. But I always had to carry a pocket full of pennies. Because the guys would scramble up there. They'd get twenty cents from this guy. And dime from that guy. Until they got that buck. And they'd come up you see. And I'd have to always give them the two cents for the tax. But you got a thousand of them up there. Bill that was a thousand dollars. So we used to pack that place up there for seven nights a week. Those days. No no no off nights then you know. And we used to pack that place. But that man couldn't. If we got fifteen people out of the hotel. We got plenty. You see.
Sure.

But he wanted me to play for the people in the hotel. I told him. I said. If I play for the people in the hotel. You ain't have nobody up there. So. We all get about it. Two three months you know. And finally I told him. I said. Look mister. Let me tell you one thing. I said. What you don't know about New Orleans will fill one book. And what you don't know about jazz will fill another book. I said. Now you want Art Hickman to get music up there. You get somebody else. Not me. I said. If I ever go there and play that way for them kids. They run me out of town. And if they would too. You come around with that chooky music with those kids. You know. They were born and raised on that music. And you had to play it for them. And we had to. Of course we didn't only play it. The boy at Dixieland now. The way they use it now. Bill had disgust me. Because we never. We played those tunes yeah. But that ain't all. We played. We played anything man. If a tune would come out of like the old swinging. The old spinning wheel you know.
Yeah sure.

We'd play the tune. But we'd play it our way. We'd play it in the New Orleans way. You know. And swing it. And so we used to have a sign on the piano. That you can't stump us. I had a regular sign up on the piano. Made out of some kind of glass. It was the first time I ever saw that. Like the sparkle. Oh yeah.
Like that you know.

And I had that up on the piano. And we could play any way. If we didn't know the tune. We'd get you to hum it to us. You know. If we got the eight bars. That's all we needed was the first eight bars. Cause the channel would take care of itself. You know. Use number one. Number two. Number three. Middle. And. requests that we can't fill or something, you know, something like that. And it come up and we didn't know the tune, somebody in the band didn't know the tune, we'd say, well, hum it to us, you know. And then, all we needed was the first eight bars, the channel would take care of itself, you know, use number one, number two, number three, middle. And then, that's how I come to the leave up there. Now, where do we go from here?
What was your first record that you ever made, I wonder?
First record I ever made was with Johnny Hyman.
With Johnny Hyman?
Yeah.
And what did you play?
I played drums.
Drums on that record. Did you do anything else?
No, that's all.
There's some singing on some of those. Huh? There's some singing on some of those Johnny Hyman songs. Oh, I don't know.

I don't know. I don't know. Maybe some of the ones that we made up at WSMB. But this was for Victor. Yeah. Uh, Alligator Crawl. And that band was Dias, Horace Dias on piano. Nappy LeMond on the guitar. Elroy Mays on clarinet. Charlie Hartman on trombone. Johnny and myself. And, and, and, huh? A bass? No bass. No.
And what were you on?
And the kid playing, Alvin, Alvin Gertro playing harmonica. Guy playing harmonica like a cornet.
Did you work with that band or was it just?
No, that band was just made up for, for, for that recording. Oh, I, Johnny worked in, in Schilling's band. That was just about the time that we were both playing with, with Schilling.
Was there a particular style you were aiming for in that record, the band?

Johnny was aiming for, for Red Nichols. Uh huh. That's before he, that's before he started imitating Bix. Uh huh. He imitated Nichols. He used to try to play exactly like Nichols. So that's, the arrangements were built around Nichols. That's about, about the time when, when Red was making all those, uh, records with the,
Five pennies and all, yeah. With the pennies.

He used to call it, used to call it futuristic, instead of calling it progressive or modern like they call it now, they used to call it futuristic music. And if you play it that way, you know, you, uh, you ahead of time. Used to try to, 된 stuff with stuff stuff with stuff with stuff

It involved arrangements and all kind of interludes and things like that. Sidney Arden was hella on that. He always had to have a cadenza at the end of the tune, you know. It's a funny story, Bill, when we were making those recordings. We had one of those tunes there. We get to the end of it and there's a clarinet cadenza. Well, when we made them, I had an infected toe, so I was using a stick. See, in a shoe, open shoe like this. And I had one of those big Chinese gongs, you know. So I had to hit one lick before the cadenza and another lick after the cadenza. And I didn't have a mallet. See, so I took a handkerchief and wrapped it around a drumstick, you see. And I had to hold it up like that. The gong, I didn't have a stand for the gong. I held the gong up like that. We made that thing in a warehouse. It's a, you know where Barnett's is now? Well, you know that little place they got on the side of the store where they sell appliances? No, not a lot. It's only a, it's a one-story building. Well, that's where we made them, because that's where Brunswick bought Calendary, the billiard people, who were the same people who made those Brunswick records. They were originally a billiard. They made billiard tables. Well, that's where their, that's where their storeroom was, you see. And that's where we made the records. It was a warehouse. That was on the left? Yeah, I'm not letting left yet. And what they did, they just hung up a bunch of cloth as drapes, you know, and made the, made the recordings right in there. And so I was holding the gun and I hit it, see, but when I hit it, the handkerchief flew off of the stick. It flew across the room, see. I had to get up like this and hobble on and grab the, grab the handkerchief. And I didn't have time to put it back on the stick. So what I did, I took the heavy gun like that and threw the handkerchief and hit it. Oh, yeah. And it hit right on the beat. Never missed, never missed a beat. And another, another thing with that, with that session was, uh, Mickey Marco was, like I said, was playing piano with us up at the roof. And we go, we go to record and, and, uh, Mickey don't show up. He, uh, I don't know, he got peeved at something, uh, because I was using shock ears or something like that. He got peeved, so it just don't show, that's all. He don't tell me anything, you don't say he's not going to beat anything. So I'm ready to record, I don't have any piano player. And we had to, we had, we had worked a month, month and a half on those arrangements, you know. They were head arrangements, but it took us that long to, to, to work them out. And, uh, I said, now what am I going to do now? So right away we got on the phone, we got ahold of Freddie Newman. And, uh, Freddie come up and I'm conning the, the, the guy that's directing the recording date. Uh, that was his name. Anyway, I'm conning him, he wants to know where the piano player is. I said, oh, he'd be here, he'd be here. Yeah. Well, we're half hour late as it is, you see. So, finally, Freddie comes. And what we got to do before we can cut, we got to teach Freddie the tune. Before we could, the only one that he knew out of, uh, out of the four of them was High Society. And we had, we had to teach him the tunes. And we had modulations and everything, you know. We changed keys and all. And he's like, I tell you, these Sydney Iron cadenzas and all. And everything was worked up. And, uh, oh man, we had a hell of a time. But that, that, that, that thing there with the, which you call it, the goggles. But it's right on the beat, not, not, not a second.
What tune was that you used the dong on?

I think it was on Ideas. I think that, because that was Sydney's tune. Ideas was Sydney's and, uh, get with it was Sydney's. Sizzling the blues was Joke of Pryor's. And I tried to steal High Society, but they caught me.
I think that's public domain anyway, really.
Yeah, but it wasn't then. Who do you think owned it then? I don't know. Sousa's family.
Really?

Yes. Because the, uh, the guy wanted to know, you know, who, who, who, who, who's the composer of the tune. So I thought, I said, well, I don't know. That's the first time High Society had been made since Joe Oliver made it. He said, Joe Oliver made it first. Well, nobody knew who it belonged to, you know. It's just like, like, like Tiger Egg and, and the, and the other ones. Uh, so he said, well, we'll put your name on it. Uh, so he did, he put my name down as a composer. And then, then before the record came out, I got a letter from him, you know. Uh, yeah. And he said, you can't claim that High Society. And they belonged to, to, to, the, Sousa was dead by that time.
Yeah.
And they belonged to Sousa's estate.
Never did find the music though.
Yeah.
I always buy those sheet music.
Well, I saw, I saw, I saw the music on that. Have you ever heard of a band by the name of Oliver Naylor?
Yeah.
Was a band out of Birmingham. Yeah.
Yeah.

Well, Ray Badouk, Jules Badouk, and a kid by the name of Bill Krieger was a clarinet player. Worked in that band. And Bill Krieger stole the orchestration on High Society out of the Library of Congress in Washington. You see, they worked there, they worked all the way from, from, from Birmingham to Washington. That was their territory. You know, all the bands in the North States had their own territory. Well, that was not, I'll nail this territory from, from Birmingham to, to Washington. And Bill Krieger stole the orchestration of that. And their part is originally a piccolo part. It's not a clarinet part. It's a piccolo part. That's a piccolo part. It's not, it's, it's not, it's not a clarinet part at all. And what's called, piccolo says he originated, piccolo's full of bologna. He didn't originate that.
I've heard too, it was in the Susan Marsh, but I never could find the Susan music part.

He had, Bill stole it from the Library of Congress now. He had the whole locker, and it was for a military band. It wasn't for, wasn't no, it was for, it was for a military band. It's, I don't know how many parts of that. But he had the whole, the whole thing, the whole orchestration. And he stole it while he was with, playing in Washington with Naylor. That's why I, every, every time I hear, they say pico originator thing, I gotta laugh, you know. Cause I saw the, I saw the thing with my own eyes, which is piccolo part.
I was wondering about Joe Coffero's style on guitar. Where did he get that?

That's, as far as I, I didn't know any, anybody. Well he did, some things he took off Snoozer. Yeah. Cause he and Snoozer were good friends. See when I had the band at the roof, Snoozer used to come up there and sit with us, whenever he was in town, you see. He'd come up there and sit there with us and play guitar and fiddle, you know. That scratchy fiddle. You ever hear him play fiddle? Never did. Oh man, you ain't heard nothing. You ain't like they say, you ain't heard nothing until you heard Snoozer play fiddle.
Was it good or is it funny?

It was marvelous Bill, but it was the stinkinest tone, it was like Fazola playing the saxophone. Fazola was the world's worst sounding saxophone player that you ever heard in your life. In fact, cause Benny Pollock, two or three times, well not only Pollock, but Miller. And a lot of the band wanted him to play the lead, cause Fazola was a marvelous musician, you know. I mean he read the seven clefs and all. But man, the tone he got out of the saxophone, the sound of Sidney Ironman, the same Rapolo was the same way. They sounded like fish horns, it didn't sound like a saxophone, you see. And well that's the kind of a tone that Snoozer got out of the fiddle. It didn't sound like a fiddle at all, but he played wonderful, you know, jazz, fine jazz. And there's a little story there. But I could tell you Snoozer used to come over and from Bogalus and sit in with us a lot of times. So Whiteman happens to be in town. They're playing the St. Charles Theater. And in the band is Bix, Trombauer, Izzy Freeman. That's the only, only jazz men in the band. So we all go to the concert. It was in two parts there, part and then, and the intermission and then another part. Well the whole first thing they never played one note of jazz, you see. So we're in the alley, Johnny Detroit could verify this. We're in the alley, we're talking to Whiteman, you see. So I was delegated to go talk to Whiteman about getting to play some jazz. Bix and Trombauer, especially because we didn't know Izzy Freeman so well then, you know. So I walked up and told him, I said, Paul, I said, we got to have some jazz. And I looked at me and Johnny, he and Johnny Detroit were talking and looking at me like that, you know. And I said, I mean, I said, we're going to have some jazz or else. See, so he says, well, I says, we don't have anything coming up. He says, the only thing we got, we're going to play things like Metropolis and American Empower. I said, well, it's a big band, a concert band, you see. So I told him, uh-uh, man, we got to have some jazz. So I looked at Johnny and he looked at me and Johnny says, well, the guys are, I said, man, there's 200 jazz men out there. They come in here to hear Bix and Trombauer, you see. So he says, well, I don't know. I said, well, I'll see what I can do, see. So they went back in, they got on and they started off with this American Empower. And they get about five minutes in and they cuts the band off like that. See, and he walks to the front of the stage and he says, ladies and gentlemen, says, I have a lot of, I've had a lot of requests and threats for Bix and Trombauer. And Roy Barger was playing piano. He says, for Bix and Trombauer. And he turns around and he looks at them and he says, boys, you're on your own. And he walks off the stage and they didn't know what to do, you know. They never had anything like that happen before, you know. So first thing you know, Roy Barger started swamping, singing the blues. So they played, they played singing the blues and they played Melancholy Baby and a couple of things that Trombauer played. And well then everybody was satisfied then. But they wouldn't have played one note of jazz in the whole concert if we hadn't done that, you know.
But what about Snoozer? You were going to tell about how?

Well, yeah. While they were here, while Whiteman was here, Snoozer was in town. So Brownlee and I, we wanted Whiteman to hear Snoozer, you see. And I had known Whiteman from Tony Perentich, man. I was working at the halfway house with Abby and I was just learning how to play a cornet thing, you see. And I think I knew about four or five tunes. And Abby used to say, you never learn how to play a thing as long as you live. And I told him, I'll see the day when I was stuck like that, you know. And they used to stagger for lunch in Perentich, man. In other words, one man at a time off the stand for lunch. And Henry Connect was playing cornet. Well, he was strictly a legitimate cornet, no jazz at all, you see. So I'd get off at one o'clock at the halfway house, you see. I'd just get in time to relieve Henry to go for lunch, you see. And we'd play the four tunes that I knew, you see. And Whiteman happened to come in town one time and he was there and he heard me playing. He asked Tony Perentich, who's the guy playing the jazz, you see. And then Tony said, yeah, the carnet plays the drum. He plays out with Abby Bruce out there. He said, just learned how to play a carnet. Well, Paul came up and he complimented me on the horn, you see. Well, anyway, Brownlee and I called Paul and told him we wanted him to hear this Snoozer, you see. So Snoozer didn't have a guitar. He didn't bring a guitar with him. So we went up to the hotel, to the Biennale and got Joe Capriero's guitar. And we brought it and we went backstage. You see, we had Snoozer play for Whiteman. And then he knocked Whiteman out. And Whiteman would listen, he'd play a thing, especially that day. Did you ever say I used to play Tiger Rag? No. He'd wave his hands like this and he'd play with his fingers, pick with his fingers, you know. He wouldn't even touch the strings with this hand. He'd be waving there and he'd make a break, you know. And the damnedest things would come out of that thing, Bill. I believe Johnny's got some, Wiggs has got some on record, yeah. He got some on record.
Not that one, but some of the others.

Whiteman would listen, man, and he'd run up and they had a, the theater was a brick wall. And he wanted me to hit his shoulder up against him, boom, against that brick wall like that, you know, every time Snoozer would knock him out.
Yeah.

And so he told Snoozer, he said, you'll hear, you'll hear from me. And nobody paid any attention to it, you see. So Snoozer gave him my address at Karns, because Snoozer was going back to Bogalusa, you see. So Snoozer gave him my address at Karns and told him that if he wanted to get in touch with him, get in touch with him through me, you see. And I had Snoozer's address in Bogalusa. It's New Year's Eve night and we're playing, like I told you, the dinner where the blue room is. And that was a Venetian room then, I think. And we're up there and then the band's all knocked out. And strange as it may seem, Bill, in those days I didn't drink. But the whole band, New Year's Eve, Freddie Newman's men almost under the piano and everybody's loaded, you know, and nothing you could do about it. So I look at the entrance and here comes somebody who's got an overcoat on, he's got the collar up like this and it comes all the way down to his ankle, you see. And he's coming across the bandstand and he reaches in his pocket and he's got a pint of gin in each in each pocket like that. I say, oh, that's all I need, you know. A Snoozer. I had gotten a wire from Whiteman a few days before and I sent word to him over in Bogalusa, you see. And he was coming in to go to New York to join Whiteman. That's another thing I got that I had, I wish I had. I had to, it's the most pitiful letter you ever heard in your life, Bill. He wrote me, it must have been 10, 12 pages after he got to New York. And they never did put him in the band. All Whiteman used him first to take him around to these parties and entertain Whiteman's friends at these parties. The guy couldn't get any sleep at all, Bill.

Because guys like all the music, everybody that heard of him, the musicians, oh, they wouldn't go up to his hotel room, the poor guy could never sleep. But guys like Eddie Lang and all those guys, Dick McDonough was there, Carl Crest and all those guys were the big ones then. And then all the guys had the guy playing night and day and he was the kind of guy that couldn't say no, you know, never could say no to you. And did you ever see him?
Never did. Never did?

Well, Snoozer was born, when he was born, they had to use forceps. And his head was lopsided like that from the forceps. His head came to almost a point, he was a funny looking guy. It was caused by the forceps when he was born. His head come, instead of coming out like that, his head went like that. See, almost into a point. And that overcoat that he had on. Like I tell you, he went and then this letter was telling me after he was up there about a month, month or that, that he was going to quit. That he just couldn't take it anymore. They wouldn't let him sleep and he wasn't making any records and anything like that. So he quit, why didn't he come on home. Never did go out of town anymore after that.
Can you tell a bit more about him? He came from... Bogalooza. Was he born over that way?
Yeah, he was born and raised there, yeah. He's still got brothers over there.
I never did know anything.

He's got a brother that's a barber. He's got a barber shop over there. In Bogalooza. You never heard anything like it, Bill. I've heard a lot of guitar players. I've heard Lang and all those, Segovia. But nobody played like Snooza. The guy was just, he was out of the world.
Did he ever play here in the city with many of the bands?

Oh, he played, he played. Not working, not studying, but sit in. He used to come over here all the time. He would, in fact, he'd come over and he'd stay over maybe a month, two months. He used to room here on magazine. Whenever he'd come in town, he used to room right here on magazine and first. Because that's where we went and got him to bring him down there to hear white. We thought he'd have his guitar and his fiddle. He only played fiddle, too. But he didn't have his instruments with him. And his mother and his aunt was with him at that time. And they were living right here at first in magazine. Or second in magazine. But if you didn't hear him, I don't know how. I never have heard the tapes that Johnny's got.
They're pretty good.
I don't see how they could do him justice.
They probably don't do him justice.
I don't think they could do him justice.
Did he play with a picker with his finger or both?

Both. And he played jazz. He played wonderful jazz. And fast. He was the fastest man picking that I ever heard in my life. I mean, he'd make all these guys sound like they're playing waltzes. You know, that's how fast he was. And like I tell you, he used to do that and just pick with this hand here. And play the damn best thing. Yeah, boy. Then he'd turn right around and he'd play with the pick. And he'd play some beautiful things like Mighty Like a Rose and those kind of things, you know. Coquette. And play a ballad. And play, oh, most beautiful.
I noticed you were showing him as if they were left-handed. I was wondering if he were. No, no. That's I am. No, no.
He was right-handed.
I was going to ask you about your cornet. You play the cornet, though, right-handed, don't you?
Yeah. Yeah. Well, I play drums half and half. I don't play left-handed drums.
That's what I noticed.

I play half and half. I play right-footed and left-handed. See, I originally started all left. See? And then, I don't know, it was more, my right leg was better. I could keep better time with the right leg than I could with the left. And then you didn't, we didn't have those flying horse things then, you know. And so I got, I don't know how I ever did it. Just all of a sudden I changed and put the, instead of putting the snare drum over on the left where it's supposed to be, I put it on the right so I could have the right leg free, you see. And that's how I got started to play. I've had more drummers, you know, come in and look up like Krupa or Buddy Rich and those guys coming, they look up there and they're trying to figure out what I was doing, you know. You can't figure it out. The guy played half and half, you know.
Yeah.
But the cornet, I do a lot of things right-handed. I eat right-handed. There's only a couple of things that I got to do left-handed.
What about Sharky? Of course we can ask him too, we haven't interviewed him, but he plays fingers at left-handed.
Left-handed, yeah.
Yeah. Kikla Rocca used to, I guess Ray Lopez.
Ray Lopez too, yeah.
Left-handed. I just wondered if some of those fellas.
There was another guy around here, Vega. Lawrence Vega, I think his name was, he played left-handed too. Yeah.
I just wondered if some of those fellas maybe weren't left-handed and just thought that was the way to do it because they saw somebody else.

Oh, that's the end of it. A funny little story, Bill, I went, in 34, I went to Hollywood with Gene Austin, you see. Well, I'd rather eat scent for me. The guy out there by the name of Jimmy Stahl was a newspaper columnist, you see. And he wrote it. We were playing at a little private, before we went in the coconut group, played at a private. They had a lot of private clubs out there that were gambling. Places like the Clover Club. Well, we played in a place called the El Rey. And it was strictly a membership deal, you see. And this guy coming in and he saw me playing the cornet and the drums. And he was trying to figure out how I could play the drums half and half. And that's how he goes off and he writes a piece in the Los Angeles paper, you see. And he says something about the drummer, ambidextrously. I never had heard that word in my life before, you know. And I told him, I said, what's that saying about me? I said, I'll rap him, you know. I never had heard ambidextrous in my life. I thought he was saying something bad about me, you know.
How did you play the drums when you played the cornet? Just with your foot?

I played the foot, yeah. And then the whole cornet with my hands. Well, you see the thing with Austin over there. We only had four pieces, you see. And they built a special stand and pushed it back against the band, regular bandstand. Gus Ornheim had the band in there while we were out there. And we'd just play intermissions. We played ten minutes five times a night. And three times Austin would sing a couple of songs with us. And we'd play a few tunes. He played that, you ever seen him play, roll the piano in the back of his fist like that? That's the way, yeah, that's the way he played. For a kick. He plays in the black keys. There's another funny story too. We got out there and we started rehearsing. I couldn't get with him, you know. I said, man, what key you playing? What key you playing in? He says, I'm playing in the black key. I'm playing in the black keys. So I tried for half an hour. I just couldn't get anywhere near him, you know. I couldn't play in the keys. He was playing. He was playing in B natural, E natural, F sharp, C sharp, you know. So finally I told him, I said, Mr. You might as well buy me a ticket and send me back home. I can't make this. He said, what do you mean you can't make it? I said, well, I just can't make it. I said, I can't play in those keys. I said, you get my keys, but he couldn't play in my keys. So he told me, finally he says, I don't know, I don't see how you can't do it. Wingy did it. You see, so I said, oh, oh, oh. If Wingy done it, there's a trick to it somewhere. Because I know Wingy can't really know as big as his head. So I said, if Wingy did it, there's a trick to it somewhere, you see. So I kept fooling around. So finally I pulled the horn out in E, you see. And he was playing some of these days. So he started to end up. Well, that put me in the same as in the key of F. The finger was the same as the key of F. But the horn was out. Instead of being flat, it's out there, you see. So I had it. So I said, go ahead. Blow, mister. Go ahead. Do anything you want. I got you now. You blowing with me now. But I was just about ready to pack up and come back home, you know. So we'd, like I tell you, we'd play five times a night, just ten minutes. And then we had a job in the afternoon. There's a place in the back of the Coconut Grove called Aledo. It's an open air thing. They put on fashion shows and things like that out there, you see. And we worked out there. I'll tell you about this later. But anyhow, in the Grove there, the times that Austin didn't play, well, we'd just go up there and just flew around. We'd play the muskrat and Panama and bugle call them, things like that. And the guys and the gals back in the bed. Onheim had a great big man, about 18 men. And they'd holler tunes for us to play, you know. And it was funny, Bill. The first night we were in there, when Onheim would play, a few people would get up and dance, you know. But when we'd get up there and play, man, everybody looked like everybody wanted to get up. And the Meta D and the Headwaters, they were trying to shove the people off the floor. They weren't supposed to dance to us, you see. They were trying to shove them off. Well, about the second night, the boss, there was a fellow by the name of Franks, walks down and he sees them. He sees them trying to shove them people off the floor. And he hollers to the Meta, what are you doing? He said, well, they want to dance tomorrow. I said, well, let them people dance. What do you want to shove them off? The big band can't make them dance, and they make them dance? Let them dance. So they'd get out there and dance when we played. And the kids back there would be, I was Panama, Tyrae. You know?
Who was that with?
Oh, cool. The Grove.
Oh, I know where we were. We were talking about the men in the band. You were going to tell us. Yeah. You took Candy's place.

Yeah, well, I took Candy went with, I took your cigarette. Yeah, Candy Candido, he quit to go with Ted Fiorita. And that's when Gene sent for me. And at the time, I was part owner of a nightclub. Out here, originally it was the Honeysuckle, and then it got to be the Golden Pumpkin. And the place in there, it was a summer place. It drew good in the summer. Winter wasn't no good at all because right under the lake it used to get a lot of fog out there. People wouldn't come out in the winter clubs. And they had to run what you call a two-bits club. Everything was two-bits. Coke was two-bits. Sandwich, two-bits. Ice, two-bits, you know. And you had to bring your own bottle. So after the summer season was over, the old Italian fellow that owned the place, says to the fellas in the band, says, I'll give you the place. I said, you run at the place. I said, I'll give it to you. She said, you're taking my son. She had a son. So he, and I think it was Jack Otto, I don't know whether you ever met Jack. He used to be a drummer around here. Charlie DuPont and myself had the business. So wound up, at the end of the week, after we paid the band off, and you couldn't cheat, none of them, they wouldn't make a penny on the scale or anything, you know, because I had the Danton sisters playing with, the two Danton boys, you know, had them playing in the band. I think I used to make around $8, $10, maybe $12 a week for myself out of it. So I get this, I get this wire from Austin, see, so I called him. So I told him, I said, what does it pay? He said, well, this, right now, the job we're working right now pays $100 and a quarter. So I said, well, you'll have to send me some car fare. He said, it's all right. So he sent me $150, you see. And, so I sold my interest in the club, for, we used to call them oyster whites, they were white linen suit, they used to wear around here a lot. Some of them, some of the guys still wear them. Oyster white linen, I sold for, for oyster white and a pair of slacks. And, I get out there, I find out, Bill, that the, it's non-union. You see, Austin had to, he had had a review, and it broke up, that, that, that, that, that Lewis lost money, and it broke up, and he, that he owed the, the union $1,100, you see. Well, as long as we worked in it, so, after I got out there, he told us, we ain't union, you know. So I said, what the hell I'm gonna do now? Well, there wasn't no, no figuring on coming back home, because I was stuck, I was out there then, and I owed him the $150 that he sent me. So, long as we worked at this L-Rater, it didn't bother us, but when we got the job at the Grove, well, then the union grabbed us, you see. So they had us all up there before the board. So, Austin had to pay the, the $1,100, and they fined him $1,000. So they got Coco in there, and they asked Coco, did you ever belong to the union? No, sir. I said, well, no, didn't you belong to the Mobile, local, so-and-so? Yes, sir. Didn't you belong to Miami, local? Yes, sir. So they had the bass player the same way. He was a kid from Texas, and he was working around for him, and I sent for him, and got him out there, after I got out there. So, asked him the same thing. Did you belong to such-and-such union in Texas? No, sir. And they had it right there, black and white. They knew they were lying, you see. So, they sent him out, and they called me in there. He said, you ever belong to the union? I said, yes, sir. I said, what union? I said, local 174. He said, why'd you quit? I said, I didn't quit. He said, what you mean, you in the union now? I said, yeah. But I said, here's my card. Paid up in New Orleans, you see. I said, what you doing working out there with this non-union outfit? So, I told him, I said, mister, if a man made you come 2,000 miles away from home, and you come out there and find out it was non-union, what would you do? So, I said, how much a week are you making? So, I told him, I said, well, we make 100 in the car, and that's the salary. I said, but we make $100 a week tips. And they thought I was crazy, because the scale out there, I think, in those days, this is 1934, I think the scale was...

around $35 a week and I told them they didn't believe me. I told them I said well I didn't lie to you so far why should I lie to you about that? So it wound up that they fined Coco $250 and they fined a bass player $250 and Austin $1,000 and $1,100 they had to pay back. They didn't fined me a dime. So I got you know just by telling the truth I got by without having to pay anything. So with this place in the back that we played in the afternoon we played from 12 to 3. So we had Coco, myself, the bass and we had two fills and a viola and had Stan Reitzman on piano. Stan was just club dating around. He had been working with Hank Hal Halstead you know and they weren't doing anything. So I got Stan to play piano and Austin didn't come there at all. He didn't sing at all in the afternoon. So we worked out things just to have the fiddles and the viola just play sustain things and figures and things like that and we had to broadcast for half an hour too. And I'd take courses on the mellow phone and on the cornet and Coco would take courses on the guitar and the piano see. So we had enough jazz there for the other. And the other guys just saw them. So the phone rings one day and Ed Wade had called me and the phone said somebody wants to talk to you. You want to talk to me. So I get on the phone. The minute I open my mouth Eddie Miller hollers I knew it was you. It couldn't be nobody else but you Pollock's band had just flew in. That's where they broke up. Of course out there then. And they had flew in and they happened to turn the radio on in the hotel you know. And they heard this music and they heard the mellow phone. They knew it wasn't there. It couldn't be anybody else but me. And when they heard where it was coming from he called me there.
Well now where we go. I was wondering about when Mares came back from Chicago with the Rhythm Kings.

Yeah. Did he play any jobs around there? Yeah. They uh... I played two jobs. Joe's got the uh... Do you ever go around by Joe's place? Once in a while. Well he's got the ad for this one night. Well I played two nights with him. We played one night at the New Orleans Athletic Club and the other night at the Italian Hall. And it was after that that the band broke up. That's the last two jobs that they played as a band. Before that though they had gone over. They went over to Mobile and they worked over at Mobile for about... Well I guess five or six months. As the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. They had over there they had Leo Addy. Steve Lycanna. And the kid that's got the best job in Chicago and he's headed for... He just signed a... When we were up there. When I was up there with Shoggy. He just signed another ten year contract. He had been there ten years before that. At that Ambassador to the East in Chicago. You know anything about Chicago? Well that's the class job in Chicago. The Ambassador to the East. Dave Lewinners. Do you know of him? Piano player. Dave Lewinners. Dave Lewinners. He's been there... He's going on twenty years now. On that one job. Yeah. Well they sent... They sent all the way to Chicago to get Dave to come down there. And to play with them and they ain't even got a job. So he went to... He worked with Tony Peretti at the Levita. Do that. Yeah. He worked with Tony. After that they went over there and they couldn't do any good over there. They stayed over there about four, five, six months. Didn't do any good so they come back home. And Dave went to work with Tony Peretti there at the Levita and then he went back to Chicago. But that's the... That was the last two... That was the last two jobs that the Rhythm Kings played as a... As a unit. And there was Paul Rapp, Steve Loiskaner, Red Long, because Lewinners was working with Peretti. And Chink Martin. And myself. Ah, Santo. Santo Antrono.
Who made the records? Do you know?

Yeah. The ones they made here, you mean? Uh, uh... August Schillang on drums. Uh... Santo, Rap. Well now they made... They made two sessions here. They made an OK session here and they made a Victor session here. The OK was with Santo, Rap, Paul... Steve Loiskaner, Freddie Newman, piano, and Chink. And a tenor? Lester. Lester Bouchon. Yeah. And the drums? August Schillang. Yeah. The Victor date, it started out with the same band, but Rap, Old Man King was the recording you used. You ought to know about him though. You know about him? I don't remember. Oh, he was the son of a gun. Man, he was one of the sticklers for being in tune and that, you know. The Victor. I seen him in California. We were making a date the same time as Ellington was making a date in California. I seen him keep Ellington from 8 o'clock in the morning until 6 o'clock at night without making a side. Because he couldn't get the band in tune. He thought. So what happened at this date with the Rhythm Kings is they didn't have... They didn't have Freddie Newman. They had Red Long on the piano. And they had Rap and Charlie Cadilla. No, Charlie wasn't there at the beginning. So they were playing and every time Rap would get a chorus, he'd get up and hit one of those P-Wistle notes, you know. And he'd blow the... That was before the electric. They had blow the needle off the wax, you see. And Old Man King kept telling him to quit playing those high notes, you see. And to tell Rap to quit doing anything, well, you just might as well talk to the King of England, you know. Who does he think he is? You know, so they finally wound up, they run Rap out of the studio. That's just before we went to the Bug House. So they run Rap out of the studio and they got a cent for Charlie Cadilla. So it wound up Charlie Cadilla made the date. On the Victor. That date.
The others were all the same? They only made... I mean the others were all the same, the drummer and all. Yeah. No, no, no, with the...

On the Victor date. No, with the Victor date, Leo. Leo Eddie. Right. Because they made that right after they come back from Mobile. They made the Victor date first and then they made the OK. That's the one with the Golden Leaf Strut and Crying For Me. They made on that.
Did you ever play play play night on any records?
Yeah, with Austin. But I never... I asked Bill about that. You remember I asked you about that a long time ago?
Oh yeah, that's right.

The day that I left Austin, see we were supposed to go to Europe. And I wanted to come home before I went to Europe and they were gonna go up and down the west coast playing vaudeville, you see. And I didn't want to do that so I told him I said well I'll go home and I'll meet you in New York. We were supposed to go to England because he had been a big hit over there at one time. And so the day that I left, the day before I left rather, we made 16 sides for Vocalion. Now the only one I ever heard, and I made 8 of those I made on cornet. And the only one that I ever heard was Chinatown. The tune. China. That's the only one I ever heard. Now I asked you, I asked a hundred people, you know, try to find them for me. Cause it's the only things I ever made on cornet. I mean on a professional label on the witch corn. Now I gotta, I gotta think back there that I played the blues with Martha Boswell playing the organ. You know these little church organs, like little home organs like that. We played the blues. She playing the organ and me playing the cornet. Then I got that thing that I, I don't know whether you gonna like this or not Richard. I don't like to say these things but they're true. That thing that you, that the original, your theme song. Oh yeah. Yeah, your, your, your, I made the original on that. Oh but, Joe Mareza's got it, it was made up at WSMB. With Johnny? Yeah. That's my tune.
Oh. Well, what about Perini? You recorded it too.
Yeah, but mellophone. I didn't make any, any cornet.
No cornet. Drums too?

I made a bunch of them in New York. Now, I went to, when I, I went to work New York, I first went to work in a, a laundry. You know these Chinese, they used to call them laundries. Well I worked in the laundry for about six, seven months. And then I went to work with a fella by the name of Jack Pettis, who originally played with the Rhythm Kings. And then went with Ben Burnie. Well after he left Ben Burnie, he made up his own band. So I went to work with him. Perini was in the band. And this boy that committed suicide, the, Donnie Pottle, bass player, he's, he's from here. He's Ralph Pottle's brother. He jumped off the bridge there. He was in the band. And, uh, Charlie Butterfield, he did, makes a lot of these network programs. You know the brothers, they're from, yeah. And, uh, who else was in, somebody else was in the band from New Orleans. It was a big band. Well we, we, we were working for Irving Mills. Irving Mills at that time controlled every record date in New York. And he controlled all the vaudeville. And the, the bands. He controlled all, all of that, you see. Well I went to work with Pettis. And, uh, we used to make, Bill, we used to make us five or six record dates a week. We, the, there was only the big four then. And then they had this one place way downtown in New York. They used to make all of these little labels. Perfect, Black Swan, O'Reo, oh they must, they must have had 50 labels. Yeah. They were all made at this one place. Then you had, you had O.K., Columbia, Brunswick, and Victor. Well Victor used to make everything, he didn't make anything in New York. He used to make everything at Camden. And, uh, well we made for those, for the big four. And then we used to make a bunch of them for the, so Irving Mills took a light in him. He heard me playing. And I used to scat sing in those days. He went, that's what he really went for. He went for the scat singing. And, uh, he take and put me in, like I told you, he controlled it. He had Ellington at the time. He had Callaway. He had the Mills Blue Ribbon. He had some kind of Sweethearts, a girls band, big colored girls band. He had every big jig band in the country, he had them all tied up. He was like Gabler. And, uh, he put me with these different bands, like we, we, we, uh, we did a date. We were making a record and, uh, there's a fella by the name of Goof Moyer that used to play mellophone and saxophone. I don't know whether you ever heard of it. Well, uh, they had hired Goof to play mellophone on this record date. See, but Goof didn't play any of them. See, but Goof didn't play anything but straight. He just played the straight lead, you see. So after we made one, one, one test, uh, Pat Astorin said, no, he says, I want you to take off. See, so, man, we played again. God did the same thing. He played the lead right straight through again, you see. So Jack says, hey Mark, where's your mellophone? I said, it's at the house. I think we were on Fifth Avenue around, around 49th, 50th Street, somewhere around this way. I think we were at Victor. We were at Victor, because I know, I can associate this with it. So he said, uh, go home and get your mellophone. So he went out to whoever the guy that had the record for the day, they told him, I said, man, I got a drummer who played more mellophone than that guy. So I went home and I got the mellophone and I wound up making the date. So while we were making the date, who comes in the studio but Red Allen and a couple other jigs, and they were making, they were making a record with Ethel Waters. She sang blues in those days. That's about the time she sang all those things, get up off your knees, you know, and all those. Yeah. And, uh, they come in there, they heard, they were, Red said, as soon as I heard the beat, I knew there had to be somebody from down home, you know. So they come in there, so I wound up going with the mellophone, leaving, finishing up our date, and then going over there and making, making the, making the date behind, behind Ethel Waters with them.
You're all on a lot of mistakes. Yeah.

And all I meant, like I tell you, I was making five or six dates a week, you see, so I was letting, I wasn't getting, collecting the money, I was letting it pile up, so I said, well, I'm gonna, you know, to myself, I'll let that pile up, and I'll be for my, for my vacation when I go home, you see. So I know somebody said, uh, said to me, all the guys used to hang on 48th and Broadway there. Yeah.
Still in Clay Center there.

Somebody said, Sam, I'm up there, man, you must be getting plenty of money, eh? I said, well, I'm doing all right. He said, well, you're getting your money? I said, well, no, I'm letting it pile up, I'm gonna, when I go home. So the guy laughed at me, you know. I said, well, what do you mean? So I said, but you, if you know what I know, you better get your money. So I went, I went up to see the guy, you know, and, uh, about three times, every time I go there, he wasn't in, or he's in conference, you know, that, that old guy, you see. So I get full of, I get full of that gin, no matter where you bought it, it was all the same gin. Every apartment house had its bootleg, you know. So I get full of gin one night, we were playing Vardville, you see. It would be through around 10, 11 o'clock at night. So I get, I get lowered and I stay awake. I stay awake.

So I go down to the office and I look back and I see him sitting back in the office with his feet up on the desk, you see. And the receptionist tells me he's busy. He's in conference. I said yes, I slammed the data open and walked out to him, look I want my money. So he laughed at me, you know. I said I want my money. Don't fool with me if you fool me but don't fool with my money, you see. So I said, what you gonna do? I said what I'm gonna do, I'm gonna go to the union, that's what I'm gonna do. So I said go ahead. So I'll go to the union, see I'm gonna file a claim. So what you think they tell him at the union? You don't belong. In those days the booking agents of that didn't have to belong to the union like they do now. He said he don't belong to North South North. I said well man I've been making all these records, I've been making five or six records a week for this guy. The only money I collected was the ones that I made with Pettis. So he said well I'm sorry, there's nothing we can do. He said the guy if he belonged to the union we could do something about it but he don't belong to the union. So that was it, I don't mind, I must have made 50, 75 dates for him. Other than the one with, do I have any of them? No. Did you collect any of them? No, I never collected a dime. Only the ones that I made with Pettis. Because then Pettis would pass by the week and if we made some out of that week, well he'd pass. And in those days it was only 30 dollars for a record date, you know. But instead of being three hours, it was two hours. The best you could make would be three sides at one sitting.
Do you remember any of the tunes that you made for Pettis?

Well, that's another thing Dick. See each one of those, each one of those big companies had what they called house names. They had a name called the Knickerbockers, they had a name called the Campus Boys, they had the Charleston Chasers, the Lads Black Aces, Bailey's Lucky Seven, Ted Wallace and his Campus Boys. Oh, they had about 15 different names, you see. And every band that recorded would record on the, for instance if you had a good band, and you were contracted to, to, to, to Victor. Well then you couldn't record for Columbia or O.K. or Brunswick. So what they would do, they would get the same band, see like, like Nichols was, was tied up, the Memphis Five was tied with Victor. The Arkansas Travelers was another one of them, Miffin made a whole lot of them. They'd use these different, what they called house names, you see. Now they might, they might have five or six bands recording under that, under that same name. So you don't know what it was yours, unless you could tell by, by what they were playing, if you remember the tune or anything like that. But that's some of the names that we were called. But there were ones with Pettis, they were Victor. He was, he was supposed to be exclusive, Victor. Victor. And the name of the band was Jack Pettis and his Pets.
Yeah, he used his own name on it.
Yeah, on, Now that's, that's, that's the only one, but the rest of them, I don't, and I don't have one of them.
And you don't remember who was in Pettis's band by the chance.

Tony, like I told you, Tony Perrani. And, uh, we had a carnet jazz carnet player, a guy by the name, uh, uh, he had played with, boy he was a jig, but he, he played with all, he was white as you are. Uh, Nigga Moore was his name. He was famous for his hat, you know, the, the derby with the growling, you know. He, he was famous for that. And then we had a kid out of Whiteman's band, Frankie Cush, played lead. Trompett, didn't, in those days he never had no five brass, he only had three brass. Uh, Charlie Butterfield on, on trombone. And, uh, his brother Walter, saxophone. And, uh, uh, Chubby McGrath, uh, Chubby McGrath, uh, Fulton McGrath is his right name. You might, you know him, he's done, he played with Goodman and all those guys in the swing area. He was on piano. And, Bonnie Pottle on bass. And the guitar player was from New Orleans, but I can't, I can't think of his name. Wasn't Jack Kuhn. Oh. Johnny Plant. He played, played viola and he played guitar and banjo. He was on, on that band. And, uh, I'm trying to think of the other saxophone players. It was a regular, vaudeville like. That's all we did, we played vaudeville. And, uh, had dance team, you know, and a comedian. A regular unit, you know, a whole unit. And we played, we played around New York. Without even leaving New York, we played over a year. That, that's how much vaudeville had going in those days.
About what year was that, do you remember?

I think that was, it was either, either 29 or 30, Bill. Because I went up there at the latter part of 27. And I think that was, and I, I worked over this, this laundry for seven, eight months or better. And, uh, and then I went with Pettis.
Say, something I wanted to get. What was that, Stan's, the drummer's name that you talked about?
Emil.
The Emil Stan, that one.
Yeah. He worked in that band in the palace, the Santo. That's where Santo started.
And some other, uh, drummer, they used to tell me about, I don't know his name, played vaudeville here. Do you remember anybody sensational that you can think of?
Happy. Call it though.
No, it was quite so.
Well, Stein was the only, he was the only one. He was the only one. He was the only one.
What was Happy?
He was the only one that, that, that, that ever attempted to play jazz. Huh?
What did Happy play like? Drums?

Oh man, Happy was, Happy was a player. Happy played drums and, and, and, and solophones. He played on the boat with, with Faith and him. He played the Lyric Theater. They used to have a, Lyric Theater right on the corner of Burgundy and, and Aberdeen. Well, they used to bring acts in like, like reviews, colored reviews, you know, like Ethel Wallace. She, she's the one that took, uh, what's called them away from here, that, uh, had a guy around here by the name of Jackson. Willie Jackson. Oh yeah. She took them away with me and brought them to New York, made an MC out of him. And, uh, well they used to bring some fine acts down there.
What if I asked the Monk, well who did he play with?

Well he played with, uh, he played with Rhythm Kings, like I told ya. And they had a band for years. They played at the, at the, the first little club. You see there was two little clubs there. The first one was right on the corner of Dryads and Common. Well they had a band in there with, uh, fiddle, bass, piano, and drums. And, uh, Johnny Beisdorff's brother, a cousin, I don't know whether his brother is, I think it's his cousin. Leonard Beisdorff. He was another black, black key piano player. He played piano. And, and Oscar played fiddle. And, uh, they had the little Angelo Parmesan on, on Badger and Chink. And they worked there for, I don't know how many years. Cause in those days Dick, you didn't, you didn't stay last maybe four, five weeks, six weeks. You stayed, I like that, I worked nine years at the halfway house. See, just the halfway house alone. And then, I worked with Abbie at the, at the, at the Metri Inn. For about three years. That was a gambling house. And I worked with him at the Silver Slipper for about three years. Well, no, if you had a good band, you went on a job, you stayed there for, indefinitely, you know. For years and years. Just like that, that P-Rod, he must have been twenty years out there at the, what's it called? Spanish Fort.
Spanish Fort.

And, uh, the halfway house, the Burnts was a tradition out there. It couldn't be the halfway house without, I think, I, I don't think there's anybody else ever played in there. But Abbie. I think after, after Abbie left, they closed up. Made an ice cream pallet out of it.
And who did Bill Crego play with?

He played with, with Naylor. Well, but here, he had the band, that's the, he, he's the first band I worked with in the quality. He had the band at the old Abson house. Uh, see, not, not where the bar is, of the old Abson, but in the, in the, in the back where Piron plays. I'm not, I mean where Pichon, where Fats plays. Well, that was the club, you see. And it was owned by two different people. The bar, well, that's the original bar across from the famous door. That's the bar that was at, at Arberville Street. And, and, and that guy owned the, but Tony DeFranco was the fellow that owned the, the club in the back. And all that was, all that was doing probation, you see. And, uh, we had, uh, Bill Crego, a fellow by the name of Joe Lambious, was a banjo player. And, uh, Red, Red Long, no, no, a fellow by the name of Joe Garrow, was a piano player. He played, he played wonderful, wonderful, uh, time, and good, real good beat, but don't ask him to take chorus, cause he couldn't take chorus to save his life. He's, uh, like a guy that I, I worked for in New York, an arranger. That, make a sit down and write, he'd, he'd, he'd make a whole arrangement, Bill, on the, on the way home on the subway, you know. Sit down there without piano, without an instrument, anything else, and make out a whole arrangement. And I see him make arrangements that Pollock's band couldn't cut. Benny, you know, take him, let the bands play him and sell him to the different band. And he brought a couple of things around there to band, I'm talking about when Benny Goodman and all those guys were with Pollock. And the band just couldn't cut his arrangement. And the guy couldn't take the chorus, don't ask him to take the chorus. He, but, sit, didn't play those chords, you know. He had a real good fine beat, but just couldn't, couldn't play by himself, that's all.
Well, we might ask about drum solos and style of playing drums, the way it used to be and the way it is now. We only have another minute, unless you have something dictated. No, that's not.

Well, we, we, uh, uh, Baby Dodge was the drummer on the boat, you see. And Ray Badu, Leo Addy and myself, the three of us, we used to all go in there, we'd copy all the Baby's licks. So at that time, if you hear, if you heard any one of the three of us, you heard the same thing, because we all played the same, the same licks. But there was never any drum solos, Bill. You got two bars, you got four bars at the most. There was never anything more than, more than four bars. And that's, that's why I can't stand drum solos today.
The drums played?

Because we were, we were taught that the drums were supposed to be felt, not supposed to be heard. And if you played loud, they called you mule foot, you know. You wasn't, you wasn't supposed to play all that. Just loud as you could play. You were supposed to work for the band, instead of, uh, and you are, you had to be even, even, even below the piano, so the piano could be heard, you know. Yeah. So that you didn't interfere with it. As long as you didn't interfere with anybody, well then everything was fine.
Well I think that's about all we got on here. Another ten seconds we'll be through. I think we covered everything pretty well. We did pretty well.

segments.title: Birth, father in Fisher's band, first teacher Rag Baby Stevens
segments.summary: Hazel gives his birth date and place, says his father was a bass drummer in Fisher's Ragtime Military Jazz Band, and names Rag Baby Stevens as his first teacher and the Rex parade as his first job.

segments.title: Personnel of Fisher's band in the Rex parade
segments.summary: He says Fisher's was the only band in the Rex parade that swung and lists its members, with himself on snare drum.

segments.title: Father's death and the torpedo-stick incident at his first parade
segments.summary: He gives his father's name and age at death, then tells how a boy hit him with a torpedo stick and Rag Baby struck the boy with a rubber-ball beater.

segments.title: Bass drummer's place in the parade band; Alessandra
segments.summary: They discuss where the bass drummer marches and the instrumentation of the Fisher band, including peck horn player Alessandra.

segments.title: First saxophones in New Orleans and the Mexican band's Ramis and Lopez
segments.summary: Hazel recalls Remus/Ramis, the Mexican band saxophonist who stayed in the city, and the cornetist Lopez, plus young George Schilling as an early saxophonist.

segments.title: Rag Baby Stevens's bands and the lodge dances
segments.summary: He lists the early ragtime military jazz bands Rag Baby played in and the lodge halls where they gave dances.

segments.title: Rag Baby's alimony troubles, later life, and comparison with Stein
segments.summary: Hazel tells how he had to finish jobs when Rag Baby fled detectives, and judges him a better band drummer than showman Stein.

segments.title: Double drums, early traps and the first hi-hat
segments.summary: He explains that double drums meant two men, describes cymbal attachments on the foot pedal, and credits Ray Bauduc with the first low hi-hat.

segments.title: Wood blocks, tom-toms and the old Chinese crash cymbal
segments.summary: He describes the percussion accessories used in jazz and the 22-inch Chinese crash cymbal he used on early records, later stolen.

segments.title: Bass drum sizes for dances and parades
segments.summary: He gives typical bass drum sizes, his own 16 by 30, and the narrower drums colored parade drummers used.

segments.title: The first foot pedal and Emil Gonzalez the drum repairman
segments.summary: Hazel describes the earliest bass drum foot pedal in detail and recommends Emil Gonzalez, a drum mechanic and collector who might still have one.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy and the river towns
segments.title: Tom Brown, Brownlee and Abbie Brunies; meeting Emmett Hardy
segments.summary: He recounts first playing with Brownlee and Abbie Brunies, then meeting Emmett Hardy at school in Gretna and forming a boys' band; Hardy died at 21 in 1925.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy and the river towns
segments.title: Emmett Hardy's family and how he started on cornet
segments.summary: Hazel describes Hardy's musical family and his custom-made convertible trumpet/cornet.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy and the river towns
segments.title: Manuel Mineta, the High Society variation and Hardy
segments.summary: He says the High Society cornet variation originated with Manuel Mineta, who taught it to Hardy, and that Red Allen got it by copying Hardy's version.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy and the river towns
segments.title: Hardy's band replaces Sharky at the Taunty social club; the free-for-all
segments.summary: Hardy's band is hired at a social club after Sharky's firing and a free-for-all breaks out, leaving Hazel hit by a bottle.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy and the river towns
segments.title: Escaping the Algiers feud and playing the Midway
segments.summary: They escape a gang from the river towns, and he describes the Midway, chicken wire and the blues in three tempos.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy and the river towns
segments.title: Owls Hall, the ferry landing and Jack Lane's trap drumming
segments.summary: He describes rough dances across the river and the only time he saw Jack Lane play trap drums.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy and the river towns
segments.title: Pansy Lane's band and the Pluto Blues at the Grunewald cave
segments.summary: He says he never played with the elder Lane but did with Pansy, and tells of the band's stunt at the hotel cave.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy and the river towns
segments.title: Abbie Brunies's clowning and practical jokes
segments.summary: They discuss Abbie Brunies as a heckler, and Hazel warns him not to try his tricks.

segments.title: Starting on drums, his mother's objections and the hocked snare drum
segments.summary: Hazel tells how his father bought his snare drum, later pawned it, and how he found it again at a marching club and began professional playing at about 14.

segments.title: The Boswell trio and joining Eckert's Jazz Band
segments.summary: After his mother smashed his drums he sits in with a band on a truck, quits his bellhop job, buys drums and plays Woodman's Hall for a year.

segments.title: Cave nightclub that did not pay and Mrs. Melanson's dances
segments.summary: Nappy Lamar's booking pays almost nothing and Hazel needs a detective to retrieve his drums; another dance hostess keeps profits from homebrew.

segments.title: Smoke wagon slang and the first time he heard the word jazz
segments.summary: He defines 'smoke wagon' and says ragtime gave way to the word jazz that he cannot trace.

segments.title: The Fisher card and Red Long's New Orleans Swing Band
segments.summary: He says the word jazz was on Fisher's 1911 card and that he played in Red Long's New Orleans Swing Band at the Ritz decades before Goodman.

segments.title: Fisher's family, the band photograph and recording logistics
segments.summary: They discuss where Fisher's relatives live and a band photograph; the recording location, date and those present are stated.

segments.title: The Big 50 club photograph and members of Fisher's band
segments.summary: Hazel explains where the picture of Fisher's band came from, how drummer Swift drowned, who was in the band, and Fisher's real name.

segments.title: Happy Schilling and his son, Fisher's change of name
segments.summary: They sort out that the saxophonist was Happy Schilling's son, and Hazel speculates on why Fisher used another name.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy, Bix and the Rhythm Kings
segments.title: Hardy leaves with Blossom Seeley's act and joins Carlisle Evans in Davenport
segments.summary: Hazel tells how Hardy and Rappolo toured vaudeville, broke up in Rockford, and joined Carlisle Evans where Bix first heard Hardy.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy, Bix and the Rhythm Kings
segments.title: Chicago union exam, Bix sits in, and Hardy's illness
segments.summary: The Rhythm Kings enlargement at Fry's Inn is ended by the union exam; Hardy teaches Bix his methods, then Hardy falls ill with TB.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy, Bix and the Rhythm Kings
segments.title: Hardy's death from periodontitis
segments.summary: Hardy dies weeks after surgery and Hazel says the certificate named periodontitis rather than TB.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy, Bix and the Rhythm Kings
segments.title: The Wolverines record and Hardy's drive and style
segments.summary: Hazel played the Wolverines record for Hardy, who identified Bix and Louis Black; he describes Hardy's legato style, New Orleans drive and refusal of Whiteman.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy, Bix and the Rhythm Kings
segments.title: Hardy's last playing, the gift of his horn and his funeral
segments.summary: At Hardy's birthday he plays the blues with his mother, gives Hazel his cornet, and dies soon after; a huge funeral crosses by ferry.

segments.chapter: Emmett Hardy, Bix and the Rhythm Kings
segments.title: Louis Armstrong's claim about Hardy and the steamboat High Society contest
segments.summary: He tells of a card from Louis after Hardy's death and of the boat contest where Louis called Hardy the king.

segments.title: Locations of the Pup, Ritz, Haymarket and Lavida
segments.summary: He sorts out the dance halls on Iberville Street and the Lavida on Burgundy.

segments.title: The district after Storyville closed
segments.summary: Hazel says places with music stayed open until about 1929 and mentions Tom Anderson, Willie Piazza and the Entertainers.

segments.title: Piano players of the district: Steve Lewis and Piron
segments.summary: He names Steve Lewis and others as the best pianists back of town and says Lewis played with Piron.

segments.title: Over the Rhine at Spanish Fort and the Piron society band
segments.summary: He describes Spanish Fort amusement park, the restaurant where Piron's society band played, and its limited jazz.

segments.title: Photograph of Jimmy Dorsey's band and the first jazz radio discussion
segments.summary: Looking at photographs, Hazel identifies Jimmy Dorsey's band members and a first radio discussion of jazz in New Orleans.

segments.title: Photograph of the Silver Slipper band and its players
segments.summary: They study a 1925 picture of a Silver Slipper band, identifying Jules Bauduc, Oscar Marco and doubling on several instruments.

segments.title: Joe Caprara's big band, Brownlee photo and the piano-shaped vibraharp
segments.summary: Photographs show Joe Caprara's large band and Brownlee's, with a vibraharp built like a piano.

segments.title: Photographs of Happy Schilling's band, Austin and Wiggs
segments.summary: Hazel identifies the Boswell girls and Happy Schilling's Halfway House band, with drummer Leo Addy, and other pictures with Austin and Wiggs.

segments.title: Records made with the Halfway House band
segments.summary: He recalls tunes cut with Schilling's band including Barataria and Pussycat Rag, and who played saxophone and clarinet.

segments.title: Mickey Markle and ragtime piano
segments.summary: They talk about pianists Bill Whitmore and Mickey Markle, the only pianist recorded with the Halfway House band, and Abbie's liking for rags.

segments.chapter: Mellophone, Brunswick records and the West End Roof
segments.title: Learning the mellophone and the Brunswick records under Sharkey's name
segments.summary: Hazel explains why he took up mellophone, and that he led the band on his Brunswick sides but hired Sharkey Bonano to record because he lacked nerve.

segments.chapter: Mellophone, Brunswick records and the West End Roof
segments.title: Bienville Roof, the Slipper fire and quitting Jules Bauduc's band
segments.summary: He explains where the Bienville and West End roofs were and how he left Bauduc's band after the Slipper fire and his stolen car.

segments.chapter: Mellophone, Brunswick records and the West End Roof
segments.title: The West End Roof manager who wanted Art Hickman music
segments.summary: Hazel tells how he quit when a new manager demanded society music, and describes the 'you can't stump us' sign.

segments.chapter: Mellophone, Brunswick records and the West End Roof
segments.title: First recording with Johnny Hyman and the Red Nichols style
segments.summary: His first record was with Johnny Hyman, with named players, patterned on Red Nichols's 'futuristic' music.

segments.chapter: Mellophone, Brunswick records and the West End Roof
segments.title: Brunswick session in the warehouse, the gong and the missing pianist
segments.summary: He tells of recording in a storeroom, rescuing the gong stroke with a flying handkerchief, and teaching Freddie Newman the tunes.

segments.chapter: Mellophone, Brunswick records and the West End Roof
segments.title: High Society copyright and Bill Krieger's piccolo part
segments.summary: He tells how Sousa's estate blocked his composer credit and that Bill Krieger took the orchestral piccolo part from the Library of Congress.

segments.title: Snoozer Hall's tone and Whiteman's St. Charles concert
segments.summary: He describes Joe Capraro's guitar influences and Snoozer Hall's fiddle tone, then how he pressed Whiteman to play jazz at his concert.

segments.title: Playing Snoozer for Whiteman backstage
segments.summary: Brownlee and Hazel borrow a guitar so Whiteman can hear Snoozer, who knocks him out; Hazel recalls how he first met Whiteman.

segments.title: Snoozer goes to New York with Whiteman and quits
segments.summary: Snoozer arrives on New Year's Eve, is kept up entertaining Whiteman's friends, and writes that he is quitting.

segments.title: Snoozer's background and fingerpicking style
segments.summary: He gives Snoozer's Bogalusa origins and his speed, finger picking and ballads.

segments.chapter: Handedness and Gene Austin in California
segments.title: Playing drums half and half; left-handed musicians
segments.summary: He explains his unusual right-footed, left-handed setup and they note left-handed players like Sharkey and Ray Lopez.

segments.chapter: Handedness and Gene Austin in California
segments.title: The 'ambidextrous' newspaper item in Hollywood
segments.summary: Hazel tells how a columnist wrote about his drumming and he misread the word ambidextrous.

segments.chapter: Handedness and Gene Austin in California
segments.title: Playing with Austin at the Coconut Grove
segments.summary: Austin plays in the black keys, Hazel solves it by pulling his horn out, and the small band outdraws Gus Arnheim's big band.

segments.chapter: Handedness and Gene Austin in California
segments.title: Leaving his nightclub to join Austin and the union fine
segments.summary: He sells his interest in a club for Austin's offer, then finds Austin's group is non-union and the union fines him.

segments.chapter: Handedness and Gene Austin in California
segments.title: Afternoon band at the Grove and Eddie Miller's phone call
segments.summary: The union penalty is settled, he plays afternoons with fiddles and viola, and Eddie Miller hears his mellophone on the radio.

segments.title: The Rhythm Kings' last jobs in New Orleans
segments.summary: He tells of two final jobs with the Rhythm Kings, their stint in Mobile, and Dave Winer.

segments.title: Rhythm Kings Victor and OK recording sessions
segments.summary: He describes the two sessions in New Orleans, Rappolo's high notes, and who played.

segments.title: Sixteen Vocalion sides with Austin and his cornet records
segments.summary: He recalls the Vocalion sides, his cornet playing, and the theme tune from WSMB.

segments.title: New York: laundry job, Jack Pettis and Irving Mills record dates
segments.summary: He tells of work in New York, joining Jack Pettis, record dates and a mellophone session behind Ethel Waters.

segments.title: Letting record pay pile up and failing to collect from the contractor
segments.summary: He leaves his pay uncollected, then the union says it cannot act against a contractor who was not a member.

segments.title: House names on record labels and Jack Pettis and His Pets
segments.summary: He explains how companies used pseudonymous band names and says the Pettis recordings were under his name.

segments.title: Jack Pettis's band and a year of New York vaudeville
segments.summary: Hazel lists the players in Pettis's band, and says they worked vaudeville for over a year about 1929-30.

segments.title: Emil Stein and Happy Bolton, New Orleans theater drummers
segments.summary: They discuss Stein's drum set-up and Happy Bolton, who played drums and xylophone in the theater.

segments.title: Long engagements: the Halfway House and the Metairie Inn
segments.summary: He recalls house bands and his nine years at the Halfway House with Abbie Brunies.

segments.title: Bill Crego's band and pianist Joe Garrow
segments.summary: Hazel names members of the band at the old Absinthe House and describes Garrow's arranging and limited soloing.

segments.title: Drum solos then and now; drums to be felt, not heard
segments.summary: He explains that drum solos were rarely more than four bars and drummers were taught to stay below the piano.

segments.title: Closing of the tape
segments.summary: Allen says the tape is about to end.
